sides.text: NAT purpose
Translates private addresses to public ones, conserving IPv4 space and hiding internal addressing
NAT terms
Inside local: private host address. Inside global: its public address. Outside global: remote host's public address. Outside local: how the remote host appears inside

more.text: The inside addresses are the ones you translate.

sides.head: Example
sides.text: PC 10.1.1.5 browses a web server 198.51.100.7 through a router with public address 203.0.113.1. Name the four addresses.

more.head: Answer
more.text:
Inside local 10.1.1.5
inside global 203.0.113.1
outside global and local 198.51.100.7
more.extra: Inside addresses belong to your network; outside addresses to the remote host

sides.text: Static NAT
One-to-one fixed mapping, used for servers that must be reachable
sides.code:
interface g0/0
 ip nat inside
interface g0/1
 ip nat outside
ip nat inside source static 10.1.1.10 203.0.113.10

sides.text: Dynamic NAT
Maps inside hosts to a pool of public addresses first-come, first-served
sides.code:
ip nat pool PUB 203.0.113.20 203.0.113.30 netmask 255.255.255.0
access-list 1 permit 10.1.1.0 0.0.0.255
ip nat inside source list 1 pool PUB

more.text: The pool can run out.

sides.text: PAT (NAT overload)
Many inside hosts share one public address using different source ports
sides.code:
access-list 1 permit 10.1.1.0 0.0.0.255
ip nat inside source list 1 interface g0/1 overload

sides.text: NAT verification
show ip nat translations, show ip nat statistics, clear ip nat translation *

more.text: debug ip nat shows live translations.

sides.text: NTP
Synchronizes clocks over UDP 123 in a stratum hierarchy

more.text: Stratum 0 reference clocks, stratum 1 servers, each hop adds 1. Accurate time matters for logs and certificates.

sides.text: Configure NTP client and server
A client points at a server; a router can act as a server with ntp master
sides.code:
ntp server 192.0.2.10
! or as a server:
ntp master 3
! verify:
show ntp status
show ntp associations

sides.text: NTP strata
NTP servers use very precise clocks and offer time to other hosts; the stratum number indicates accuracy — lower is more accurate

more.text: A host using its own clock as a source sets its own stratum; a host getting time from another sets its stratum to one higher than its source.

sides.text: NTP client and static client mode
ntp server address configures a device as an NTP client

more.text: Cisco devices set as NTP clients automatically also act as NTP servers themselves for others — "static client mode".

sides.text: NTP master and broadcast client
ntp master [stratum] makes a device offer its own clock as a time source, defaulting to stratum 8

more.text: ntp broadcast client makes an interface listen for NTP broadcasts from any server. ntp server and ntp master can be combined for redundancy: the device uses the external server but falls back to its own clock if that connection fails.

sides.text: NTP on a loopback interface
Preferable to using a physical interface's IP for NTP: a loopback is a virtual interface that's always up (unless manually shut down)

more.text: If a physical interface goes down, services bound to its IP become unreachable via any path; a loopback IP stays reachable via any surviving path, provided it's advertised in the routing protocol. Set with "ntp source loopback 0".

sides.text: NTP authentication

ntp authenticate enables it
ntp authentication-key key-number md5 key defines an MD5 key
ntp trusted-key key-number trusts it
the client's ntp server command references the key ID it expects the server to sign with

more.text: On the NTP server, only ntp authenticate and ntp authentication-key are needed.

sides.text: DHCP role
Automatically provides IP address, mask, gateway, DNS, and lease

more.text: Messages: Discover, Offer, Request, Acknowledge (DORA); Discover is a broadcast to 255.255.255.255 (UDP 67/68).

sides.head: Example
sides.text: A PC on VLAN 10 gets no address; the DHCP server is on another subnet. What is probably missing?

more.head: Answer
more.text: ip helper-address on the VLAN 10 gateway interface
more.extra: Broadcasts do not cross routers without a relay

sides.text: DNS role
Resolves names to IP addresses

more.text: Record types: A (IPv4), AAAA (IPv6), CNAME, MX, NS, PTR; UDP/TCP 53.

sides.text: DHCP relay
A router forwards DHCP broadcasts to a server on another subnet as unicast
Router as DHCP client or server
A router interface can learn its address, or serve a pool
sides.code:
interface g0/1
 ip address dhcp
!
ip dhcp excluded-address 10.1.1.1 10.1.1.20
ip dhcp pool LAN
 network 10.1.1.0 255.255.255.0
 default-router 10.1.1.1
 dns-server 8.8.8.8

sides.text: DHCP message exchange (DORA)

Discover (client→server, broadcast)
Offer (server→client)
Request (client→server, broadcast)
Acknowledgment (server→client)
DHCP relay
A router forwards DHCP messages between clients and a centralised DHCP server, since routers don't forward broadcasts by default

more.text: Configured with ip helper-address server-ip on the interface facing the clients; it sets the giaddr field so the DHCP server knows which subnet the request came from.

sides.text: Router as a DHCP client
(config-if)# ip address dhcp

more.text: When DHCP provides a default gateway, it's inserted into the routing table as a static route with Administrative Distance 254.

sides.text: DHCP server configuration

ip dhcp pool name enters the pool context
network address mask specifies the subnet to hand out addresses from
ip dhcp excluded-address excludes a specific address or range
default-router and dns-server set the options clients receive
SNMP roles
Network devices are SNMP agents, gathering information as variables in a Management Information Base (MIB)

more.text: Agents exchange information with SNMP managers, typically Network Management Station (NMS) servers, which poll agents and compile/present the data.

sides.text: SNMP polling vs notifications
Managers usually poll agents with Get/GetNext/GetBulk Requests, and agents respond with Get Responses

more.text: Agents can also proactively notify managers via Traps (UDP, no reliability — if lost, it's lost) or Informs (added in SNMPv2, reliable — the agent expects an acknowledgment and resends if none arrives).

sides.text: SNMP MIBs and OIDs
MIB variables are identified by tree-structured Object IDs (OIDs), given as either numbers or names, e.g. iso.org.dod.internet.private.enterprise.cisco.ciscomgmt.ciscoflash.group (1.3.6.1.4.1.9.9.10)

more.text: Part of each MIB is standardised in RFCs; the rest is vendor-defined.

sides.text: SNMP versions
SNMPv1 and SNMPv2c use communities — pre-shared passwords exchanged in cleartext

more.text: SNMPv3 adds authentication with a username and hashed password, message integrity, and optional encryption.

sides.text: Syslog logging targets

Console (users on the console port)
Monitor (Telnet/SSH users, who must run "terminal monitor" to actually see messages)
Buffer (logged to RAM, viewed with "show logging")
Syslog/host (sent to a remote syslog server)
Syslog severity levels

1 Emergency
2 Alert
3 Critical
4 Error
5 Warning
6 Notification
7 Informational
8 Debug

more.text: Filtering by level shows that level and everything more severe (lower-numbered); "debug" shows everything.

sides.head: Example
sides.text: logging trap warnings sends which levels?

more.head: Answer
more.text: 0 through 4

sides.text: Syslog message formatting
service timestamp enables/disables timestamps on log messages; service sequence-numbers enables/disables sequence numbers
IOS debugging
The debug EXEC command enables detailed logging for a specific service, generating severity-7 messages sent only to targets with that severity enabled
QoS purpose
Gives different applications their required treatment during temporary periods of network congestion, based on their sensitivity to bandwidth, delay, loss and jitter

more.text: Real-time traffic like voice and video is very sensitive to delay, loss and jitter even though it needs comparatively little bandwidth; batch data traffic is not.

sides.text: QoS classification and marking
Classification identifies packets by matching header fields; marking tags them accordingly. Neither affects forwarding on its own — only a policy acting on the marking does

more.text: Best practice is to classify and mark as close to the source as possible (ideally the access switch), so devices further along can just trust the marking.

sides.text: QoS trust boundary
End devices other than IP phones or Telepresence units shouldn't be trusted to mark their own traffic, since that would let rogue users prioritise their own traffic

more.text: mls qos trust cos extend trust to a connected device's markings (common between switches); switchport extend cos n instructs an attached IP phone to mark its PC port's traffic with a given (often 0/best-effort) CoS value, overriding the PC.

sides.text: QoS marking fields

DSCP (Differentiated Services Code Point): 6 bits in an IPv4/IPv6 header (Layer 3), backwards compatible with IP Precedence
CoS/PCP: 3 bits in an 802.1Q tag (Layer 2, trunk links only)
IP Precedence: 3 bits, superseded by DSCP
TIP: 3 bits in an 802.11 header
EXP: 3 bits in an MPLS label
DiffServ marking classes

Expedited Forwarding (EF/DSCP 46): low loss, delay and jitter — used for voice
Assured Forwarding (AFxy): 4 queues (x, 1=worst to 4=best) × 3 drop priorities (y, 1=best to 3=worst)
Class Selector (CSx): maps old IP Precedence values to DSCP

more.text: Recommended usage: EF for voice, AF4y for interactive video, AF3y for streaming video, AF2y for high-priority data, CS0 for standard best-effort data.

sides.head: Example
sides.text: Which DSCP value is used for voice?

more.head: Answer
more.extra:
Expedited Forwarding:
low delay
low loss
strict priority queue

sides.text: Queueing and congestion
Queueing only happens when a link is congested, e.g. a speed mismatch between an incoming Gigabit interface and a slower outbound WAN link

more.text: A standard queue with no QoS policy uses FIFO (First In First Out), which can let voice packets get stuck behind bulk data during congestion.

sides.text: CBWFQ and LLQ
Class-Based Weighted Fair Queueing (CBWFQ) gives a minimum bandwidth guarantee to specified traffic classes during congestion

more.text: Low Latency Queueing (LLQ) is CBWFQ plus a strict priority queue, whose packets always jump to the front — ideal for real-time voice.

sides.text: LLQ priority queue limits
The priority queue's bandwidth share is capped, defaulting to a maximum of 33%, and going above that isn't recommended

more.text: Otherwise the priority queue could starve all other traffic entirely (100% usage would leave 0% for everything else). Call Admission Control (CAC) on voice servers can limit concurrent calls so the priority queue never actually needs more bandwidth than it's been given.

sides.text: Traffic shaping vs policing
Both measure traffic rate through an interface and act if it exceeds a configured limit

more.text: Shaping buffers excess traffic to smooth it to the desired rate (typically used outbound by customers); policing drops or re-marks excess traffic to enforce the limit (typically used inbound by service providers on customer-facing interfaces).

sides.text: Congestion avoidance — tail drop and global synchronisation
Tail drop happens when an outbound queue is full and further packets are simply dropped

more.text: This shrinks the TCP windows of all affected flows at once ("global synchronisation"), so they all slow down and speed up together, underutilising the link.

sides.text: RED and WRED
Random Early Detection randomly drops packets before a queue actually fills up, at a rate based on how full it already is, to signal individual flows to slow down before congestion peaks

more.text: Weighted RED (WRED) extends this by dropping lower-priority packets more often, breaking global synchronisation while also protecting more important traffic.

sides.text: Wireless QoS service levels

Platinum: VoIP, CAPWAP control tunnels
Gold: video, mission-critical interactive traffic
Silver: best-effort, the default
Bronze: guest services
Configure SSH

Hostname and domain
RSA keys
local user
vty transport
sides.code:
hostname R1
ip domain-name lab.local
crypto key generate rsa modulus 2048
ip ssh version 2
username admin secret Str0ng!
line vty 0 15
 login local
 transport input ssh

sides.text: FTP connections
Uses two TCP connections: control (port 21 by default) and data

more.text: In active mode, the client opens the control connection then tells the server (via PORT) to connect back to a client-chosen port for data. In passive mode, the client sends PASV and the server tells the client (via PORT) which port to connect to for data. A NAT or firewall between client and server can break FTP unless it supports FTP application inspection.

sides.text: FTPS
FTP Secure — FTP built on TLS encryption

more.text: Explicit mode uses one port (21) for both connections, starting in plain FTP and upgrading via an AUTH command (backwards compatible). Implicit mode connects straight to ports 990 (control) and 989 (data) in TLS, with no explicit AUTH.

sides.text: SFTP and TFTP
SFTP (SSH File Transfer Protocol) is unrelated to FTP but serves the same purpose, using SSH (port 22) for encryption and authentication

more.text: TFTP (Trivial File Transfer Protocol) is a stripped-down protocol on UDP port 69, with very basic application-layer error recovery, resulting in slow transfers.

sides.text: IOS file systems
Types include Opaque (aliases), Network, Disk (flash drives), Usbflash and NVRAM (used for startup-config by default)

more.text:
show file systems lists them
dir shows a directory's contents
show flash shows the default flash file system
copy copies files
verify /md5 checks a file's MD5 hash

sides.text: Copying files over the network in IOS

copy tftp dest launches the TFTP client interactively
copy ftp://user:pass@host/filename dest runs the FTP client in batch mode

more.text: ip ftp username / ip ftp password set default FTP credentials so they don't need to be typed in the URL each time.

sides.text: TFTP vs FTP
TFTP: UDP 69, no authentication, simple. FTP: TCP 20/21, authenticated, reliable

more.text: Use SCP or SFTP for secure transfers.
